A B S T R A C T
Post-earthquake fires in populated stations pose a significant threat to passenger safety, neces­
sitating the implementation of efficient emergency evacuation procedures to adequately safe­
guard lives and property. Utilizing Building Information Modeling (BIM) and Pathfinder, this
study innovatively delves into the emergency evacuation optimization measures under a post-
earthquake fire. Three pivotal research questions are explored: a comparative analysis of the
Required Safe Egress Time (RSET) versus the Available Safe Egress Time (ASET) to evaluate the
safety of evacuation procedures; a focused examination of critical time points and influential
factors during evacuation process; and the formulation of optimization measures to enhance
evacuation efficiency. The Beijing Xiyuan rail transit station was chosen as a case study, with four
post-earthquake fire scenarios simulated. Additionally, the impact of obstacles and injured
personnel resulting from the earthquake was considered. The results show that: (1) During
evacuations, critical issues arise at specific time points. The entrances of escalators/stairs, turn­
stiles, and exits are key sites, where congestion becomes critical issues. (2) Evacuating rescue
personnel through public non-paid areas saves 9.1 % of the evacuation time compares to crossing
turnstiles. (3) The most impactful measures for optimizing evacuation is that trains arrive in only
one direction, followed by the deployment of evacuation guidance. Thus, key control time points
and optimization measures for the evacuation process of complex urban rail transit stations can
be obtained. The findings provide insights and guidance for optimizing emergency evacuation in
rail transit stations to mitigate post-earthquake fire risks and ensure public safety.
1. Introduction
In recent years, earthquakes have presented high frequency all over the world, causing significant economic, environmental, and
social destruction, and posing a great threat to people and settlements [1]. 183 Ms 7.0 earthquakes occurred around the world from
2012 to 2024, resulting in lots of casualties and economic losses [2]. For example, on February 6, 2023, a Ms 7.8 earthquake struck
Türkiye, followed by another of the same magnitude 9 h later, resulting in the loss of over 59,000 lives in Türkiye and approximately
8500 in Syria, with direct economic losses estimated at around 100 billion dollars [3]. Except for the disastrous consequences directly
induced by earthquake, secondary hazards are also triggered to worsen the problem [4], such as post-earthquake fire. In recent years,
post-earthquake fires still perform a common and threatening disaster, especially after a devastating earthquake [4,5]. Most of these

casualties, up to 80 %, were caused not by the earthquakes themselves, but by the subsequent fires [5]. Post-earthquake fires, often
triggered by damaged electrical equipment, ruptured gas lines, and spilled fuel in earthquake, have significantly higher potential [6].
For example, the 1906 San Francisco earthquake resulted in at least 700 fatalities, and the subsequent fires ravaged over 500 city
blocks, leading to widespread destruction. The direct economic losses were estimated at 4 billion dollars [7]. The Japan Kobe Ms 7.3
earthquake caused 269 fires due to natural gas leaking and 7036 buildings were destroyed in the post-earthquake fires in 1995 [7].
Thus, the research of post-earthquake fires becomes particularly important.
In recent years, various kinds of complex urban public spaces with multi-layer structures and crowded clusters have been con­
structed and operated in the urban context, such as complex rail transit stations, integrated railway transportation hubs, and airport
terminals [8]. The complex rail transit station, as a pillar of the urban transport infrastructure system, possesses the capability to
accommodate a large number of passengers and has become an essential way for people to facilitate transportation [9]. China has
continued to occupy a leading position in the field of urban rail transit. By the end of 2023, urban rail transit has been established in 55
cities across 31 provinces in China, encompassing a total of 306 operational lines. Additionally, 5897 stations had been opened, with a
total operating mileage of 10,165.7 km [10].
However, with the expansion of the scale of rail transit systems, rail stations in many cities have become populated spaces,
especially transfer stations with multiple rail lines. In the existing research, 62 risk events were documented for the rail stations, with
25 identified risks and 241 risk interaction chains extracted, among which the sensitivity of earthquake ranks 12th. Therefore,
earthquakes are one of the important risks that endanger the safe operation of urban rail transit stations [11]. The densely populated
rail transit stations are vulnerable to the impact of earthquakes, which is particularly serious during the morning or evening rush hour
or when sudden large passenger flow occurs [12]. For example, approximately 50 % of daily passengers prefer to use rail transit during
peak hours in Beijing. Besides, the ridership during weekdays is twice as high as it is during weekends [13]. What’s more, due to the
characteristics of underground structures, such as a lack of natural ventilation, light, and direct connection to the outside, it makes it
more difficult for passengers to evacuate during fire [14]. For instance, a fire in the King’s Cross Station in London killed 32 and injured
more than 150 people in 1986; the Daegu metro fire killed at least 198 people and injured at least 147 on February 18, 2003; and the
Baku subway fire in the Republic of Azerbaijan caused more than 340 casualties in 1995 [15–17]. If a post-earthquake fire occurs in a
crowded setting, it may cause significant safety hazards. Meanwhile, the complex structure and high population density on each floor
pose significant challenge for evacuation during the fire [18]. Therefore, it is crucial to ensure that evacuees are well-informed and
utilize the most efficient evacuation routes in the prompt evacuation to reach a safe place during post-earthquake fires [19].
The primary aim of this research is to delve into four distinct emergency evacuation scenarios in rail transit stations during post-
earthquake fires, with a focus on identifying and developing optimized evacuation measures that guarantee the safe and swift
evacuation of individuals. This research revolves around three principal questions: Firstly, it employs the RSET derived from Path­
finder to compare with the ASET, in order to assess whether evacuees can safely evacuate from the rail transit station. Secondly, the
results garnered from Pathfinder are utilized to undertake a deeper analysis of critical time points and influential factors during the
evacuation process. Finally, it explores the emergency evacuation optimization measures, which encompass the implementation of
evacuation guidance, the removal of movable barriers, and the reduction in the number of arriving trains. The composition of this
research is as follows. The second section contains the literature review. The third section describes the methodology, including the

2. Literature review
The review is conducted in three distinct aspects: emergency evacuation, emergency evacuation in rail transit stations, and research
methods. Table 1 offers a comprehensive summary of the studies pertaining to these three facets.
2.1. Emergency evacuation
Evacuation planning and scheduling is a critical aspect of disaster management and national security applications, which is of great
significance in ensuring public safety and reducing potential losses. Many scholars have conducted research on emergency evacuation.
Zheng et al. [20] proposed a game-theoretical model to study evacuees’ cooperative and competitive behaviors during an emergency
evacuation, which determines the density of evacuees and their related evacuation times. Shan et al. [21] analyzed the key factors that
impact the emergency evacuation in fire outbreak, flooding, and flood coupling scenarios. Abdelghany et al. [22] presented a simu­
lation optimization modeling framework for the evacuation of large-scale pedestrian facilities with multiple exit gates. Given the
limited capacity of safe spots, Khakzad et al. [23] utilized mathematical programming to determine the allocation of people to each
safe spot and the optimal evacuation path, aiming to minimize the risk of casualties based on the Dijkstra algorithm.
2.2. Emergency evacuation in rail transit stations
Rail transit stations are underground structures with limited entrances and exits, intricate interior layouts, narrow transfer pas­
sageways, and limited stairs and escalators. These factors, along with the presence of various facilities and equipment, pose challenges
to emergency evacuations. Yu [24] analyzed fire evacuation capacity factors in rail transit systems and developed a safety evacuation
assessment index system, quantifying indicators through virtual reality technology, computer simulation, and on-site investigation.
Zhang et al. [25] established an evaluation indicator system that includes 16 indicators of human, equipment, environmental, and
management factors, and evaluated the emergency evacuation capability of rail transit stations. Shiwakoti et al. [26] explored the
likely behaviours of train passengers in an emergency evacuation and examined four crucial theoretical issues on the passengers’
evacuation. Jia et al. [27] proposed a multi-objective optimization model and employed the NSGA-II algorithm to effectively balance
theoretical validity with computational efficiency for urban rail transit stations. VanLandegen et al. [28] combined GIS-based network
analysis with microsimulation techniques to develop a framework for simulating emergency evacuations using rail transit.
2.3. Research methods
The traditional evacuation drill method has several drawbacks, such as high costs, lengthy time consumption, susceptibility to on-
site conditions, low accuracy in evacuation outcomes, and significant safety risks. In contrast, computer simulation and modeling can
effectively reduce costs, save time, and are less influenced by on-site conditions. Thus, computer simulations have been adopted to
study emergency evacuations in rail transit stations. Huang et al. [29] proposed an evacuation route-planning algorithm based on
predicted traffic conditions to expedite evacuation from a disaster area. Deng et al. [30] established a dynamic route optimization
method for obtaining the real-time optimal evacuation route. Guo et al. [31] proposed a VR simulation method for indoor fire
evacuation that enhances route planning efficiency by using 3D scenes and character models combined with environmental factors.
Zhong et al. [32] adopted a dynamic personnel evacuation model to simulate fire evacuation in deep-buried rail transit stations,
assessing the feasibility of safe evacuation. Chen et al. [33] established a simulation model for pedestrian evacuation in subway fires
using Legion and FDS(Fire Dynamics Simulator) software to enhance evacuation capabilities during the planning, design, operation,
and maintenance stages. Guo et al. [34] proposed a hybrid approach integrating BIM(Building Information Modeling), AnyLogic, and
machine learning algorithms for evacuation event simulation and proactive evacuation management. Qin et al. [35] used Pathfinder
software to simulate the evacuation process in a rail transit station, analyzing the evacuation under various conditions by configuring
fire scenarios and adjusting flow rates.
In summary, there are numerous simulation and modeling software applications available for emergency evacuation, among which
Pathfinder has a higher degree of agent intelligence [36]. Pathfinder is specifically designed for simulating emergency evacuations
with highly realistic three-dimensional models and behavior simulations [37]. It supports the import of results from FDS and provides
clear visualization of complex disaster scenarios, making it well-suited for simulating fires in large scale infrastructure with different
layouts and escape routes. Therefore, Pathfinder is applied in this research for simulating and modeling purposes.
2.4. Gap in research
According to existing studies, the following three research gaps can be identified:
(1) There has been relatively less attention given to the emergency evacuation of post-earthquake fires in rail transit stations. The
potential for post-earthquake fires in buildings poses a significant threat to occupants, first responders, and the structural
integrity of the station. Therefore, it is crucial to evacuate passengers promptly from densely populated rail transit stations
under a post-earthquake fire to mitigate the risk of serious injuries and fatalities.

(2) Existing studies lack exploration of the key elements for optimizing emergency evacuation in complex rail transit stations. This
study discusses the critical elements for optimized evacuation measures in the complex rail transit station, including adaptable
evacuation guidance, movable barriers, and the number of evacuees.
(3) Existing evacuation studies mostly rely on static settings. This study specifically analyzes the effects of different evacuation
scenarios dynamically, such as trains arriving from multiple directions simultaneously, the presence of evacuation guidance and
movable barriers, etc. The primary focus is on analyzing evacuation time under these diverse scenarios, which can guide the
development of more effective emergency evacuation measures.
3. Methodology
The research framework is shown in Fig. 1. The Building Information Modeling (BIM) and Pathfinder software are adopted in this
research. Then, four scenarios are assumed for emergency evacuation simulation. In the research, the Beijing Xiyuan rail transit station
was chosen as a case study. Based on the BIM modeling, the RSET obtained from Pathfinder is used to compare with the ASET obtained
from the previous publications to assess if evacuees can safely evacuate from the rail transit station. The critical time points and
influential factors during the evacuation are analyzed. The impacts of obstacles and injured personnel within the passageway and exit
resulting from earthquakes are introduced and simulated. Additionally, the proposed three evacuation optimization measures are
implemented in the station.
3.1. BIM
BIM is growing globally in the fields of architecture and engineering. BIM is an important technology in the construction digita­
lization world, which can be used by adopting computer visualization technology and simulation method [38]. The IFC (Industry
Foundation Classes) standard enables the precise specification of building and construction data. By exporting BIM models crafted in
Revit into the IFC file format, the integrity of building data can be accurately preserved. Furthermore, these imported files can be used
in Pathfinder software to conduct evacuation simulations in fire emergency scenarios. In essence, the IFC format facilitates a smooth

3.2. Pathfinder
Pathfinder evacuation simulation software is developed based on agent-based models for simulation calculations, which is suitable
for simulating the actions and interactions of intelligent agents with autonomous consciousness. It is widely used as a simulation
software to assess emergency evacuation and escape systems for people. The model has fast calculation speed, which can handle the
evaluation and analysis of large complex buildings for personnel evacuation research [39]. The software can align with the actual
construction pattern at the architectural level and assign individual parameters to each person, such as walking speed, shoulder width,
exit selection, etc. It can also simulate the independent movement patterns of each individual.
Besides, pathfinder simulates individual movements using Society of Fire Protection Engineers (SFPE) mode and Steering mode.
SFPE allows personnel independently choose the nearest exit based on passenger flow, and Steering is a combination of path planning
and collision movement [17]. The steering behavior can also be controlled by guidance mechanisms designed to regulate the evac­
uation of individuals. In contrast, steering introduces collisions, and personnel exit choices are determined by multiple factors, making
it more realistic [40]. Therefore, this study selected the steering mode of emergency evacuation.

3.3. Assumptions in simulation
It is assumed that all load-bearing structural components remain intact after an earthquake, while some non-structural components
collapse such as metal fences. As for the fire codes in various types of buildings, it can be assumed that evacuation during a fire or other
emergency situation is carried out only through the stairs, and the escalators can be used as stairs after stopping [42]. This article
assumes that all turnstiles will be opened after an earthquake, making it easier for evacuees to evacuate as quickly as possible. Besides,
this article assumes that a post-earthquake fire occurs just as a train arrives at a rail transit station. A large number of passengers on the
train need to be evacuated, and the passenger flow on the platform floor and the concourse floor will rapidly increase [24], and the
evacuation pressure on the rail transit station is significantly intensified. The simulation of the emergency evacuation was conducted
for an accident occurring in a stationary train at the platform floor [43].
3.4. Evacuees characteristics
3.4.1. Maladaptive behavior
Most passengers typically exhibit complex psychological reactions under a fire [44]. This often affects their ability to make sound
judgments and choose effective evacuation routes. Pedestrians’ behavior during emergency evacuations often differs from normal
circumstances. As rail transit stations have complex structures and high passenger volume, evacuees during an emergency are prone to
herding behavior [45], panic behavior, and habitual behavior [46], which lead to irrational behavior.
(1) Herding behavior
The phenomenon that individuals’ directions are influenced by neighbors can be easily found in emergency situations, which is
called herding behavior [45]. Due to limited visibility and guidance, pedestrians sometimes prefer to follow the choices made by others
rather than actively seeking the optimal evacuation exit [47]. Herding behavior can be explained by the social attachment model, as
individuals in a crowd often seek the experiences of others to make evacuation decisions. However, in extremely crowded spaces,
situations with limited visibility, or when finding an exit becomes challenging, herding behavior can lead to severe congestion at a
particular exit, resulting in uneven utilization of exits [48].
(2) Panic behavior
Panic is a common emotion when pedestrians are in danger during the evacuation, which can affect pedestrians a lot and may lead
to fatalities as people are crushed or trampled [49]. Some individuals may experience panic due to the perceived threat to their lives
under fire. This can lead to a loss of judgment and blind conformity, triggering collective panic behavior. Accordingly, serious
behavioral characteristics that significantly affect the safe evacuation of individuals may emerge [50].
(3) Habitual behavior
When evacuation personnel are familiar with the evacuation environment, they may exhibit habitual behavior, where they
automatically choose the evacuation route and exit that they regularly use [51]. Such behavior often results in the emergence of
disorganized evacuation processes, characterized by the crisscrossing of passenger flow. This undermines the ability of individuals to
evacuate quickly and efficiently.
3.4.2. Shoulder width
Factors such as shoulder width of indoor personnel can have an impact on evacuation time. This study focuses on evacuation
research in rail transit stations during peak hours, where the majority of individuals are mostly adult males and adult females. Ac­
cording to existing studies [52,53], the shoulder width of Chinese adults aged 18–70 is as follows: for males, it ranges from 398 mm to
510 mm, and for females, it ranges from 361 mm to 459 mm. In the US, the standard shoulder width dimension is 22 inches (558.8
mm). In the process of designing buildings, it is reasonable to assume that the shoulder width of adult males is 50 cm, while that of
adult females is 40 cm for calculating [54]. This information serves as a reference for subsequent evacuation considerations.
3.4.3. Evacuation speed
Research indicates that the average comfortable walking speed usually varies between 1.2 m/s and 1.6 m/s [55,56]. During un­
expected accidents, the evacuation speed of individuals will be faster. The evacuation speed tends to vary significantly across different
cultures and countries, influenced primarily by regional differences. According to the investigation and analysis of the evacuation
speed of personnel, Helbing et al. [57] have recommended an efficient average speed around 1.5 m/s through their dynamical model.
Xiao et al. [39] considered that men evacuate at a speed of 1.95 m/s, whereas women evacuate at a slightly lower speed of 1.79 m/s
during the evacuation. The speed was decided to accurately represent the gender-specific differences in evacuation speeds, while also
considering the increased efficiency observed in panic situations. It revealed that the level of emotional response increases with the
urgency of evacuation while the attention and control of individuals can rapidly decrease. As a result, passengers subconsciously try to
move faster than normal [58]. The simulations conducted in this study primarily consider time frames during festive occasions or peak
commuting hours, when there is a larger presence of young individuals commuting to and from work. Consequently, this research
predominantly classifies the population into two categories: adult males and adult females. The evacuation speed for adult females is
set as 1.79 m/s, and for males is set as 1.95 m/s. Meanwhile, the possibility of individuals being injured and unable to move due to an
earthquake is also considered, requiring assistance from others for rescue. According to the existing research results, two rescuers can
assist an injured personnel at 0.6 m/s [59].

3.5. Evacuation time
The key to determining whether people can be successfully evacuated is the Available Safe Egress Time (ASET) and Required Safe
Egress Time (RSET) [60]. The “Fire Safety Engineering Part 9: Guidelines for Personnel Evacuation Evaluation”(GB/T 31593.9–2015)
issued by the National Standardization Administration of China pointed out that when ASET > RSET, it indicates that there is sufficient
time for personnel inside the building to evacuate safely. The relationship between ASET, RSET and the personnel evacuation process is
shown in Fig. 2. The determination of ASET depends on the tolerance limit of the human body. The usual method for calculating ASET
is to simulate and measure that the temperature and harmful gas concentration reaches the critical value through software simulation,
and compare and analyze the minimum critical time to determine the available safe evacuation time.
3.5.1. The available safety egress time (ASET)
(1) Temperature
Human endurance to high temperatures is limited, particularly when it can cause irreversible damage to the skin and respiratory
tract. To ensure the safety of the evacuees, the temperature must be maintained within a certain range. Research reveals that thermal
burns to the respiratory tract can occur when individuals inhale air above 60 ◦C saturated with water vapor [61]. In this research, 60 ◦C
is considered as a threshold value. The ASET for temperature is the time required for the temperature to reach 60 ◦C.
(2) CO Concentration
The primary threat to people’s life safety in a fire is the CO produced during the combustion process [62]. The proportion of
hemoglobin(HB) in the form of carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) increases steadily as CO is inhaled causing HB to lose its ability to provide
oxygen. Thus, the acute toxicity of CO depends mainly on the percentage of COHb. Survival is rare in subjects with blood levels
exceeding 50–60 % COHb and 50 % COHb is usually considered as an average lethal level [63]. When the CO concentration is 1600
ppm, the COHb (%) concentration range is between 40 % and 50 % [62]. Accordingly, 1600 ppm(1.6 × 10−3 mol/mol) is considered as
a threshold value. The ASET for CO is the time required for the CO concentration to reach 1600 ppm.
3.5.2. The required safety egress time (RSET)
The required safety egress time of passengers is primarily divided into various stages: response time and moving time (which
includes time for arriving at the stairs/escalators, time for passing the stairs/escalators, time for staying on stairs/escalators, and
passage non-uniformity deviation time) [16]. RSET is expressed as follows:

4. Case study
4.1. Spatial modeling
In China, the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei region is situated at the intersection of the Yanshan uplift, the Taihangshan uplift and the North
China Basin, making it susceptible to high seismic hazard and risk in the Chinese mainland, such as the devastating 1976 Ms 7.8
Tangshan earthquake [64]. During the Tangshan earthquake, almost all the casualties and economic losses were concentrated in
high-intensity regions including Tangshan, Tianjin, and Beijing [65]. In this research, Beijing Xiyuan rail transit station was used as the
case study. The station is located on the north side of the intersection between Yuanmingyuan West Road and Yiheyuan Road, which
presents the characteristics of complex structure, large area, high density passenger flow, and large numbers of power lines. It enjoys a
prime location surrounded by numerous attractions, including Yuanmingyuan, the Summer Palace, and Xiyuan Traditional Chinese
Medicine Hospital. Serving as a vital transfer station, it connects Line 4 and Line 16 of the Beijing rail transit, providing convenient
transfers between the two lines through a passageway that links the two concourses.
According to the “Annual Report on Transportation Development in Beijing” released by the Beijing Municipal Commission of
Transport in 2023, the total passenger flow of rail transit in Beijing reached 2.263 billion in 2022, making it the most widely used mode

4.2. Fire scenarios
In this research, the study takes into account scenarios involving the outbreak of a fire in the power distribution room, obstacles and
injured personnel, as well as multiple fires and variations in sizes, in order to comprehensively present the post-earthquake fire
characteristics.
According to statistics from the Fire and Rescue Department of China’s Ministry of Emergency Management, electrical fires have
surged by 42.7 percent in the past decade [66]. Combustible materials within rail transit stations encompass numerous components,
notably circuits and electrical equipment housed in power distribution rooms, which are highly prone to ignition post-earthquake fires
[18]. The primary focus of this article lies in identifying and examining the most vulnerable locations for fires in the aftermath of
earthquakes: specifically, the power distribution room.
Ordinary fires tend to propagate outwards from the ignition point, posing significant risks of localized congestion and potential
building collapse. Conversely, earthquakes inflict structural damage on buildings, including various non-structural elements like
suspended ceilings. This structural and non-structural damage within complex rail transit stations not only heightens the likelihood of
electrical equipment catching fire due to seismic activity, but it also results in collapses occurring at locations distant from the ignition
point. Damaged non-structural components further compound the situation, creating obstacles along evacuation routes. People may
become trapped indoors due to injuries or mobility difficulties [67]. Therefore, in this research, the collapsible obstacles created by
earthquakes are specifically considered, which obstruct the passageway connecting Exit B1 and Exit B2, as well as the exit, situated at a
distance from the ignition point.
This research assumes that the power distribution room of Line 4 is on fire. Notably, rescuing fires in the aftermath of an earthquake
is typically more challenging than dealing with conventional fires. This is due to the extensive damage often caused by post-earthquake
fires, which can lead to the concurrent occurrence of multiple fires and obstacles. To gain a deeper insight into the fire risks in rail
transit stations post-earthquake, this study takes into account multiple fires and variations in fire sizes. Consequently, two scenarios are
explored: a single-floor fire and a double-floor fire, each with varying fire sizes. Based on the size of the fire, four distinct scenarios are
hypothesized, as detailed in Table 2.

(1) Obstacles in the passageway
As shown in Fig. 7, the evacuation routes for all evacuees can be discerned. It’s evident that obstacles in the passageways con­

In Fig. 8, the first evacuee (highlighted by the red circle) in Scenario 1 entered the passageway connecting Exit B1 and Exit B2 at
85.6s due to being unaware of the obstacles. After approaching the passageway connecting Exit B1 and Exit B2 where the obstacle was

escaped the passageway at 99.2s. Additionally, during the evacuation process, one of the evacuees (highlighted by a yellow circle)
mistakenly entered the passageway connecting Exit B1 and Exit B2 at 162.2s because evacuee was unaware of the presence of obstacles
in the channel. When approaching obstacles in the passageway, the evacuees realized that the passageway was blocked and began to

5.1. The influence of evacuation guidance
When a fire breaks out following an earthquake, the crowd often exhibits herd behavior, panic, and a tendency to follow familiar
routes, leading to maladaptive actions. The identification of distinct time points during evacuation simulations was based on two
critical issues: severe congestion and confusion regarding evacuation directions. In severe congestion, facilities such as escalators/
stairs and turnstiles may accumulate a large number of people. Meanwhile, evacuation guidance can play a crucial role by providing
guidance and assistance, directing evacuees towards safe areas and reducing the likelihood of chaos and accidents.
The main purpose of setting up evacuation guidance at the entrances of escalators/stairs on the platform floor is to regulate the
evacuees flow. Simultaneously, evacuation guidance will be strategically positioned at the entrance of passageway, particularly those
obstructed by obstacles, to deter evacuees from entering blocked pathways. Furthermore, evacuation guidance at the turnstiles aims to
maintain a balanced evacuees flow through each turnstile, ensuring a smooth evacuation process. A comparison study between sce­
narios without evacuation guidance and with the evacuation guidance was conducted. The simulation results show that when trains
from four directions arriving at the station simultaneously, the passenger flow is the highest. Evacuation guidance at the rail transit
station could reduce the maximum evacuation time, as shown in Table 7.

and blockage at key points of the evacuation route. Removing obstacles can shorten evacuation time to a certain extent. For instance, in
scenario 4, the maximum reduction in time is 25.5s. Additionally, the effective control of the number of evacuees directly influences
the efficiency of the evacuation process in rail transit stations. This is evident from the data of Fig. 20, where simultaneous arrivals of
trains from three directions reduce waiting time by a maximum of 35s, followed by a reduction of 127s when trains from two directions
arrive simultaneously. Remarkably, when only trains from one direction arrive, the maximum reduction in waiting time can reach
312s. Therefore, by implementing measures to manage and regulate the flow of evacuees during emergencies, such as preventing
overcrowding, the evacuation process can be optimized for smoother operations.
The most impactful measure for relieving congestion is that train arriving in only one direction, followed by the deployment of
evacuation guidance and removing movable barriers. Taking the Scenario 1 as an example, the measure of train arriving in only one
direction saved the most time, up to 312s, resulting in a potential 44.9 % reduction in evacuation time. Additionally, trains arriving
from both directions saved 127s, optimizing 18.3 % of the evacuation time. Furthermore, adding evacuation guidance saved 226.8s in
Scenario 1, translating to a 32.7 % reduction in evacuation time. Comparing the maximum evacuation time before and after removing
the barriers in Scenario 1, 10s reduction was observed, accounting for approximately 1.44 % of the total evacuation time.
6. Conclusion
As the rail transit stations undergo expansion, numerous urban rail transit stations transform into densely populated areas,
resulting in significant passenger congestion, particularly during peak hours or unexpected spikes in passenger traffic. In the event of a
post-earthquake fire, rail transit stations with high passenger density can be exposed to significant secondary disasters that pose a
substantial threat to the safety of passengers and property. This study innovatively conducts a simulation of emergency evacuations in
complex rail transit stations under post-earthquake fires, leveraging BIM and Pathfinder technologies. Utilizing Pathfinder, the study
compares the RSET with the ASET. Subsequently, it delves into the critical time points and influential factors during the evacuation
process, drawing insights from Pathfinder’s results. Ultimately, the research explores effective measures for optimizing emergency
evacuation. The research findings include the following three aspects.

(1) During evacuations, critical issues arise at specific time points, notably at 98.4s, 157s, 168s, 226s, and 265.72s, particularly
concerning the congestion at entrances of escalators/stairs, turnstiles, and exits. Therefore, during the emergency evacuation
period, effective control measures should be taken for these key points.
(2) Evacuating rescue personnel via designated public non-paid areas significantly reduces evacuation time compared to navigating
through turnstiles. It is crucial to designate and conspicuously label these non-paid areas as primary evacuation routes, enabling
rescue personnel to circumvent turnstiles effortlessly. Furthermore, in emergency scenarios, an automated system should be
implemented to swiftly transition all revolving gates into a free passage mode, thereby minimizing congestion and enhancing
evacuation efficiency.
(3) Controlling the number of trains arriving at the station and increasing the number of evacuation guidance are two recom­
mended measures to optimize emergency evacuation.
The findings provide insights and guidance for improving emergency response efficiency and ensuring the safety of personnel in rail
transit stations. This study has reference value for the architectural design of complex structural buildings such as rail transit stations.
For example, the key location nodes and evacuation time information obtained through research can be used to optimize the archi­
tectural design, making the building perform better during emergency evacuation. In the next phase of the research, it is expected that
intelligent technology will be utilized to conduct studies on fire monitoring and early warning systems within complex structural
buildings, and that the likelihood of facility collapse within the buildings will be forecast.
